title: Culture, Migration and Identity
bigQuestion: When people and cultures move and mix, what is kept, what changes, and who decides?

story.title: Mole in Two Languages
story.kicker: In a Pilsen kitchen, a grandmother teaches a family recipe in Spanish, and her grandson answers in English.
paragraphs: On a Saturday morning in Pilsen, on Chicago's Lower West Side, Doña Rosa lays out dried chiles on her kitchen table. Ancho, mulato, pasilla. She came to Chicago from Michoacán, in Mexico, more than forty years ago. Today she is teaching her grandson Mateo how to make mole, the dark, rich sauce her mother made for every wedding and baptism.

"Primero, los tostamos, pero con cuidado," she says. First, we toast them, but carefully. Mateo is sixteen. He understands almost every word. But when he answers, it comes out in English. "Like this, Abuela? Not too long?" She nods and laughs. The two of them have talked this way his whole life, each in the language that feels most like home.

Outside, the neighborhood tells its own story. Murals of Mexican history cover the brick walls. Many of the old buildings were built by Czech immigrants more than a century ago. The name Pilsen itself comes from a city in what is now the Czech Republic. Down the street, a new coffee shop sells drinks at prices some longtime families find hard to pay.

As the sauce darkens, Mateo asks a question he has been thinking about. "If I make this for my kids someday, but I explain it in English, is it still our recipe?" His grandmother stirs for a long moment. "The recipe is in your hands," she says. "The words are in your heart. Use both."
story.think: What traditions in your family or community have changed as they were passed down? What stayed the same?

lessons.title: The Korean Wave and Anime
lessons.mainIdea: Popular culture from South Korea and Japan now reaches fans around the world, a sign of cultural globalization.
reading: In 2012 the South Korean singer Psy released "Gangnam Style." Its music video became the first on YouTube to pass one billion views. A few years later, the group BTS was filling stadiums in the United States and Brazil. In 2018 members of BTS spoke at the United Nations. Fans who did not speak Korean learned the words to their songs anyway.

This spread is often called the *Korean Wave*, or Hallyu. It began with Korean TV dramas that became popular across Asia in the late 1990s. The South Korean government and companies invested in music, film and games. In 2020 the Korean film Parasite became the first film not in English to win the Academy Award for Best Picture.

Japan's *anime*, or animated film and TV, followed a similar path. Studio Ghibli's Spirited Away won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature in 2003. Series like Pokémon and Dragon Ball became favorites for children on every continent. Manga, the Japanese comics that many anime come from, now fill shelves in American libraries.

The spread of goods, ideas and culture across the world is called *globalization*. Some people worry it will make every place the same. But the Korean Wave shows a different pattern. Culture no longer flows only from the United States outward. Smaller countries can now reach huge audiences, and fans often learn about the place the culture came from.

words.d: the growing spread of goods, money, ideas and culture across the world
the worldwide spread of South Korean music, film and TV since the late 1990s, also called Hallyu
animated film and television from Japan

look.title: One Playlist, Many Places
look.text: A student in Chicago opens her music app. Her playlist has a BTS song from Seoul, a reggaeton hit from Puerto Rico, a theme song from a Japanese anime, and a song from a Bollywood film made in Mumbai. She has never visited any of those places.
look.prompt: What does her playlist show about globalization? Does it make cultures more alike, more different, or both? Explain.

check.q: What is the Korean Wave?
choices: The worldwide spread of South Korean pop culture
check.why: The Korean Wave, or Hallyu, is the spread of South Korean music, film and TV around the world.

check.q: Which film became the first not in English to win the Academy Award for Best Picture?
check.why: The reading says the Korean film Parasite won Best Picture in 2020.

check.q: What pattern does the Korean Wave show, according to the reading?
choices: Culture flows only from the United States
Only large countries can export culture
Culture now flows from many places, including smaller countries
check.why: The reading says culture no longer flows only from the United States, and smaller countries reach huge audiences.

lessons.title: Bollywood and Reggaeton
lessons.mainIdea: Bollywood films and reggaeton music show how a local style can grow from its roots into a global one.
reading: In Mumbai, India's largest city, film studios turn out hundreds of movies a year. This Hindi-language film industry is known as *Bollywood*, a blend of Bombay, the city's older name, and Hollywood. Bollywood films are famous for long stories, big family dramas and song-and-dance scenes. India as a whole makes more films each year than almost any other country.

Bollywood travels with the *diaspora*, the people of Indian heritage living around the world. Films open in London, Dubai, Toronto and Chicago. They are also popular in places with few Indian residents, such as parts of Africa and Central Asia. Many fans love the music and dancing even if they read the subtitles.

*Reggaeton* has a different story. It grew in Panama and Puerto Rico in the 1990s. It mixed Jamaican reggae and dancehall, hip-hop and Latin rhythms, with lyrics in Spanish. At first some radio stations would not play it. By 2017, "Despacito" by Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee became one of the most-streamed songs in history.

Both styles show *cultural hybridity*, the mixing of traditions into something new. Bollywood borrows from Indian classical dance and Hollywood musicals. Reggaeton borrows from Caribbean, African American and Latin music. In each case, the new style became a source of pride for the people who created it.

words.d: the Hindi-language film industry based in Mumbai, India
people living far from the homeland of their family or ancestors
a music style that grew in Panama and Puerto Rico in the 1990s, mixing reggae, hip-hop and Latin rhythms
the mixing of different cultural traditions into something new

look.title: Trace the Roots
look.text: A reggaeton song plays at a school dance. Its beat, called dembow, traces back to Jamaican dancehall. Its rhymes and flow echo hip-hop from New York. Its lyrics are in Puerto Rican Spanish. The dancers include students whose families come from Mexico, Poland, India and Nigeria.
look.prompt: List the cultures that shaped this one song. What does that list tell you about how new styles are born?

check.q: Where is Bollywood based?
check.why: Bollywood is the Hindi film industry in Mumbai, whose older name was Bombay.

check.q: Where did reggaeton grow in the 1990s?
check.why: The reading says reggaeton grew in Panama and Puerto Rico, mixing reggae, hip-hop and Latin rhythms.

check.q: What does cultural hybridity mean?
choices: Keeping a tradition exactly the same
check.why: Cultural hybridity is the blending of different traditions into a new style.

lessons.title: Food That Travels
lessons.mainIdea: Food is one of the oldest ways cultures spread, and dishes change as they move to new places.
reading: Order chicken tikka masala in London, and you are eating a dish many Britons call a national favorite. Its exact origin is debated, but it is widely linked to South Asian cooks in Britain. Order a California roll in Tokyo, and you may be eating sushi first made popular in North America. Food changes as it moves.

Food has always traveled. Chiles, tomatoes, corn and potatoes came from the Americas. After 1492 they spread to Europe, Africa and Asia in what historians call the *Columbian Exchange*. Before that, there were no chiles in Indian curry and no tomatoes in Italian sauce. Many dishes people think of as ancient are only a few centuries old.

Today, migrants carry food with them and open restaurants in new countries. Cooks often adjust recipes to local tastes and ingredients. This process is called *adaptation*. Chinese American dishes like General Tso's chicken are quite different from food in most of China. Tex-Mex food grew from Mexican cooking in Texas.

Some people say adapted dishes are less real. Others say adaptation is how food cultures have always stayed alive. Many immigrant cooks run two menus, one for newcomers and one for people from home. Food lets people share their culture with neighbors while keeping a taste of where they came from.

words.d: the transfer of plants, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world after 1492
changing something to fit a new place, such as adjusting a recipe to local tastes
a person who moves from one place to another to live or work

look.title: Where Did Your Lunch Come From?
look.text: A school lunch tray holds a slice of pizza with tomato sauce, a side of corn, a chocolate milk and an orange. Tomatoes, corn and cacao, the bean used to make chocolate, all first grew in the Americas. Oranges came from Asia. Wheat for the crust was first grown in the Middle East.
look.prompt: How many continents helped make this one lunch? What does that tell you about how old food exchange is?

check.q: What was the Columbian Exchange?
choices: The transfer of plants, animals and people between the Americas and the world after 1492
check.why: The Columbian Exchange began after 1492 and spread crops like tomatoes, corn and chiles around the world.

check.q: Which food first grew in the Americas?
check.why: The reading says tomatoes, corn, chiles and potatoes came from the Americas.

check.q: What is an example of adaptation in the reading?
choices: Growing wheat in the Middle East
General Tso's chicken in Chinese American restaurants
check.why: General Tso's chicken is a dish changed to fit American tastes, which is adaptation.

lessons.title: Why People Migrate
lessons.mainIdea: People migrate because of push factors that drive them away and pull factors that draw them to a new place.
reading: In 1990 a young nurse left Manila, in the Philippines, for a hospital job in New York. Her pay in the United States was many times higher, and she sent part of it home each month. Her story is one of millions. The United Nations estimates that about 281 million people lived outside the country they were born in by 2020.

Researchers sort causes into two kinds. *Push factors* drive people away, such as war, poverty, disasters or persecution. *Pull factors* draw them in, such as jobs, safety, schools or family already living there. Most people move for a mix of both. The largest sources of migrants today include India, Mexico, Russia and China.

A *refugee* is a person forced to flee their country because of war or persecution. International law, including a 1951 United Nations convention, gives refugees the right not to be sent back to danger. Other migrants move by choice to work or study. Many send money home. These payments, called *remittances*, are a major source of income for countries like Mexico, the Philippines and India.

Migration changes both places. Home countries can lose skilled workers but gain money and new ideas. New countries gain workers, businesses and culture. They also face questions about jobs, housing and how newcomers fit in. Those questions are at the center of the debates in the next lesson.

words.d: a reason that drives people to leave a place, such as war or poverty
a reason that draws people to a new place, such as jobs or safety
a person forced to flee their country because of war or persecution
money that migrants send back to family in their home country

look.title: Largest Countries of Origin for Migrants
look.prompt: Which country had the most people living abroad in 2020? What push or pull factors might explain it?

check.q: Which is a pull factor?
choices: A good job offer in another country
check.why: Pull factors draw people to a new place. A job offer is a pull; the others push people away.

check.q: What are remittances?
choices: Money migrants send to family back home
Papers needed to cross a border
check.why: Remittances are payments migrants send home, a major income source for countries like Mexico and the Philippines.

check.q: About how many people lived outside their birth country in 2020, according to the UN?
check.why: The United Nations estimate in the reading is about 281 million international migrants.

lessons.title: Assimilation, Multiculturalism, Integration
lessons.mainIdea: Countries choose different policies for newcomers, from assimilation to multiculturalism to integration, and each has supporters and critics.
reading: In 1908 a play called The Melting Pot opened in the United States. Its writer, Israel Zangwill, pictured immigrants blending into one new American people. That idea is called *assimilation*: newcomers adopt the language and customs of their new country and become part of the mainstream. Many American public schools once taught this goal directly.

Canada chose another path. In 1971 it became one of the first countries to adopt *multiculturalism* as official policy. The idea is that groups can keep their languages and traditions while being full citizens. Supporters often compare Canada to a mosaic, where each piece keeps its color. France, by contrast, stresses one shared republican identity and keeps religion out of public schools. A 2004 law bans conspicuous religious symbols there.

Many countries now speak of *integration*, a middle path. Newcomers learn the language and laws and take part in work and civic life. They may keep their culture at home and in their communities. Integration is described as two-way: newcomers adapt, and the country also adapts to them.

Each approach has critics. Some say assimilation erases heritage. Others say multiculturalism can leave groups living apart. In 2010 German Chancellor Angela Merkel said her country's attempt at multiculturalism had failed, and she called for more focus on learning German. Supporters of each model point to places where it has worked.

words.d: newcomers adopting the language and customs of a new country and blending into the mainstream
a policy that supports groups keeping their own cultures while being full citizens
a middle path where newcomers join common civic life while keeping parts of their culture

look.title: Melting Pot, Mosaic or Salad Bowl?
look.text: Person A: A country needs one shared language and shared values, or people will not trust each other. Person B: People should not have to give up their language or faith to belong. Person C: Newcomers should learn the language and laws, and the country should make room for their traditions too.
look.prompt: Match each person to assimilation, multiculturalism or integration. Which reasons does each give?

check.q: Which country adopted multiculturalism as official policy in 1971?
check.why: Canada became one of the first countries to make multiculturalism official policy in 1971.

check.q: Which idea did Israel Zangwill's 1908 play The Melting Pot express?
check.why: The melting pot pictures immigrants blending into one people, which is assimilation.

check.q: Why is integration called two-way?
choices: Newcomers adapt, and the country also adapts to them
People move in and then back out
It applies only to two countries
check.why: The reading says integration asks both newcomers and the country to adapt.

lessons.title: Debates About Migration
lessons.mainIdea: People disagree about how much migration a country should allow and how, and each side raises real concerns.
reading: In a town meeting, a factory owner says she cannot find enough workers and wants more visas. A retired machinist worries that newcomers will lower wages. A teacher says her classroom is richer for the students from many countries. A nurse points out that half the aides at her hospital were born abroad. Each speaker is describing something real.

Supporters of more migration often argue that newcomers fill jobs and start businesses. They say migrants pay taxes and help aging countries with too few young workers. Many also make a moral case: people fleeing danger deserve safety. Economists have found that migrants often start new companies at high rates.

People who want less or more controlled migration raise other concerns. Some worry about wages for workers without college degrees, pressure on housing and schools, or the speed of change in a neighborhood. Many stress the *rule of law*: that a country has the right to decide who enters and to enforce its rules. Economists disagree about how large the wage effects are.

These debates are about values as well as facts. How much should a country weigh the needs of newcomers against those of current residents? How fast can a community change and still hold together? Good arguments on any side use evidence and describe the other side fairly.

words.d: official permission to enter and stay in a country for a certain purpose and time
the idea that everyone, including the government, must follow the same laws
legal membership in a country, with its rights and duties

look.title: A Right to Leave
look.text: Everyone has the right to leave any country, including his own, and to return to his country.
look.cite: United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 13, 1948
look.prompt: This article gives a right to leave a country. Does it say every country must let people in? Why might that difference matter in debates about migration?

check.q: Which argument is most often made by supporters of more migration?
choices: Countries have no right to borders
Newcomers fill jobs and help aging countries
check.why: The reading says supporters argue that newcomers fill jobs, pay taxes and help countries with too few young workers.

check.q: What does the rule of law mean in this debate?
choices: A country can decide who enters and must enforce its rules fairly
check.why: The rule of law means everyone follows the same laws, including a country's rules on who enters.

check.q: What does the reading say about wage effects of migration?
choices: Economists disagree about how large they are
check.why: The reading says economists disagree about the size of wage effects, so it is contested.

lessons.title: Saving Languages
lessons.mainIdea: Many of the world's languages are endangered, and communities are working to bring them back through schools and daily use.
reading: In 1982 a group of Māori elders in New Zealand opened small preschools called *kōhanga reo*, meaning language nests. Grandparents spoke only Māori to the toddlers all day. At that time, few Māori children spoke the language of their ancestors. Hundreds of language nests followed, then Māori-language schools. Today many more young Māori speak the language.

Experts count about 7,000 languages in the world. Groups that track them, such as Ethnologue and UNESCO, estimate that around 40 percent are *endangered*. An endangered language is one that children are no longer learning at home. When the last speakers pass away, a language becomes extinct, and with it go songs, stories and ways of seeing the world.

Languages often fade because of pressure from a bigger language used in schools, jobs and media. In the past, many governments punished children for speaking their home language at school. This happened in Indian boarding schools in the United States and in other countries. *Language revitalization* is the work of bringing a language back into daily life.

There are success stories. Hebrew was revived as an everyday spoken language in the late 1800s and 1900s. Welsh is taught in every school in Wales. In Paraguay, most people speak Guaraní, an Indigenous language that is official alongside Spanish. Each case shows that schools, families and pride can keep a language alive.

words.d: a language that children are no longer learning at home, so it may disappear
efforts to bring a fading language back into daily use
Māori-language preschools in New Zealand, meaning language nests

look.title: The Last Speaker
look.text: An elder is one of the last people who speaks her community's language fluently. She knows words for plants that are not in any dictionary, and songs sung only at harvest. Her grandchildren understand a little but answer in English. A local school asks her to teach one hour a week.
look.prompt: What would be lost if no one learned her language? What else, besides one hour a week, might help it survive?

check.q: What were the kōhanga reo?
check.why: Kōhanga reo were preschools opened in 1982 where elders spoke only Māori to young children.

check.q: About what share of the world's languages are endangered, according to experts in the reading?
check.why: The reading says groups like Ethnologue and UNESCO estimate around 40 percent of languages are endangered.

check.q: In which country is Guaraní, an Indigenous language, official alongside Spanish?
check.why: The reading says most people in Paraguay speak Guaraní, which is official with Spanish.

lessons.title: Indigenous Peoples Today
lessons.mainIdea: Indigenous peoples around the world are working to protect their lands, languages and self-government, with growing recognition of their rights.
reading: In northern Norway, the Sámi people have herded reindeer for centuries. In 1989 Norway opened a Sámi Parliament, an elected body that speaks for the Sámi on language, culture and land. Sweden and Finland have Sámi parliaments too. The Sámi still debate with governments about mines and wind farms on their traditional grazing lands.

*Indigenous peoples* are the descendants of the people who lived in a place before later settlers or states arrived. The United Nations estimates there are about 476 million Indigenous people in about 90 countries. They include Quechua communities in Peru, Māori in New Zealand, Ainu in Japan and hundreds of Native nations in the United States.

In 2007 the United Nations adopted the *Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples*. It affirms rights to culture, language and land, and to be consulted on projects that affect them. In the United States, there are over 570 federally recognized tribes. Each is a *sovereign nation* with its own government, which can run courts, schools and businesses.

Challenges remain. Many Indigenous communities face higher rates of poverty and fewer health services. Many also lead in protecting forests and rivers. Japan formally recognized the Ainu as an Indigenous people in a 2019 law. Change is often slow, but Indigenous leaders continue to shape it.

words.d: descendants of the people who lived in a place before later settlers or states arrived
a nation with its own government and the right to make many of its own decisions

words.w: Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
words.d: a 2007 United Nations statement of Indigenous rights to culture, language, land and consultation

look.title: A Right to Be Consulted
look.text: The Declaration says states should consult and cooperate in good faith with Indigenous peoples through their own chosen representatives. They should seek their free and informed consent before approving projects that affect their lands, such as mines or dams.
look.cite: United Nations, Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, Article 32, 2007 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Think of the Sámi and a planned wind farm on grazing land. What would following this article require?

check.q: What did Norway open for the Sámi in 1989?
check.why: The reading says Norway opened a Sámi Parliament in 1989 to speak on language, culture and land.

check.q: What does it mean that U.S. tribes are sovereign nations?
choices: They have their own governments that can run courts, schools and businesses
check.why: Sovereign nations have their own governments and make many of their own decisions.

check.q: When did the UN adopt the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples?
check.why: The reading says the United Nations adopted the Declaration in 2007.

lessons.title: Exchange or Appropriation?
lessons.mainIdea: People argue about where cultural exchange ends and cultural appropriation begins, especially when sacred symbols or profit are involved.
reading: In 2012 the Navajo Nation sued a clothing company that sold items labeled "Navajo," including underwear and a flask. The Navajo Nation had registered its name as a trademark. It argued that the products used its name without permission and misled buyers. The case was settled in 2016. It sparked a wide debate about who can use a culture's name and symbols.

*Cultural exchange* is the sharing of ideas, arts and customs between groups, usually with respect and on both sides. It has always happened. *Cultural appropriation* is a term some people use when members of a more powerful group take elements of another culture without understanding, credit or permission. The concern is sharpest when the item is sacred, such as a feathered headdress worn in ceremonies.

People disagree about where the line falls. Some argue that borrowing is how culture grows, and that labeling it appropriation can discourage people from learning about others. Others argue that it matters who profits and who gets credit, especially for groups that were once punished for practicing their own culture.

Many people suggest a few questions to ask. Is the item sacred to the group? Does the group get credit or share the profit? Was it shared by members of that culture? Did I learn its meaning? These questions do not settle every case, but they help people think it through with respect.

words.d: respectful sharing of ideas, arts and customs between groups
a term for taking parts of another culture without understanding, credit or permission, often debated
a name or symbol registered by law so that only its owner can use it to sell goods

look.title: Three Cases
look.text: Case 1: A Korean grandmother teaches her neighbors to make kimchi, and they share it at a block party. Case 2: A company sells costume headdresses modeled on sacred ceremonial ones and keeps all the profit. Case 3: A Japanese chef opens a taco restaurant after training with cooks in Mexico City and names them on the menu.
look.prompt: Use the questions from the reading to decide which cases look like exchange and which might be called appropriation. Explain.

check.q: Why did the Navajo Nation sue a clothing company in 2012?
choices: The company used the Navajo name without permission
The company refused to sell Navajo art
check.why: The Navajo Nation held a trademark on its name and argued the company used it without permission.

check.q: When is the concern about appropriation sharpest, according to the reading?
choices: When food is shared at a party
When a recipe is taught in class
When the item is sacred, such as a ceremonial headdress
check.why: The reading says the concern is sharpest when sacred items are used without understanding or permission.

check.q: What is one argument against calling borrowing appropriation?
choices: Borrowing is how culture grows and it can encourage learning
check.why: Some argue that borrowing has always helped culture grow, and that the label can discourage learning about others.

lessons.title: Pilsen and Chinatown
lessons.mainIdea: Pilsen and Chinatown show how immigrant communities build neighborhoods that keep culture alive and change over time.
reading: Pilsen, on Chicago's Lower West Side, was first home to Czech immigrants in the late 1800s. They named it after Plzeň, a city in Bohemia. Many brick buildings and churches from that time still stand. Starting in the mid-1900s, Mexican families moved in, and Pilsen became one of the best-known Mexican American neighborhoods in the country.

Pilsen is famous for its murals, painted on walls, viaducts and schools. They show scenes from Mexican history, Aztec symbols and local leaders. The National Museum of Mexican Art, founded in 1982, is in Harrison Park. In recent years, rising rents and new businesses have brought *gentrification*. That means wealthier newcomers move in and costs rise, sometimes pushing out longtime residents.

A few miles east, Chicago's Chinatown centers on Cermak Road and Wentworth Avenue. Chinese immigrants moved there in the early 1900s from an older area downtown. The Chinatown Gate and the Pui Tak Center, with its green-and-red tile roof, are well-known landmarks. The neighborhood has grown with newer arrivals from mainland China, Hong Kong and Taiwan.

Both neighborhoods are examples of an *ethnic enclave*, an area where many people share a heritage. Enclaves give newcomers help with jobs, language and housing. Critics once worried they kept people apart. Many residents see them as a bridge, a home base for joining the wider city.

words.d: a neighborhood where many people share a heritage, with shops, churches and groups that serve them
a change where wealthier people move into a neighborhood, raising costs and sometimes pushing out longtime residents
a large painting on a wall or building

look.title: Walking 18th Street
look.text: Walk down 18th Street in Pilsen. You pass a panadería with trays of pan dulce, a mural of Mexican revolutionaries, a Catholic church built by Czech immigrants, a new coffee shop with pricey lattes, and a sign reading "Pilsen is not for sale."
look.prompt: What clues show the neighborhood's history? What clue shows a debate happening today, and what are the two sides?

check.q: Who first settled Pilsen and gave it its name?
check.why: Czech immigrants settled Pilsen in the late 1800s and named it after Plzeň in Bohemia.

check.q: What is gentrification?
choices: Wealthier newcomers moving in and raising costs
check.why: Gentrification means rising costs as wealthier people move in, sometimes pushing out longtime residents.

check.q: Where is the center of Chicago's Chinatown?
check.why: The reading says Chinatown centers on Cermak Road and Wentworth Avenue.

lessons.title: Devon Avenue and Ukrainian Village
lessons.mainIdea: Devon Avenue and Ukrainian Village show how many communities, faiths and generations can share and shape one city.
reading: On Devon Avenue, in the West Ridge neighborhood on Chicago's North Side, one block may hold a sari shop, a Pakistani restaurant and a Kosher bakery. Since the 1970s, many immigrants from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh have opened businesses there. Earlier, the area was home to a large Jewish community, which is still present. Some stretches of the street carry honorary names for Gandhi and for Muhammad Ali Jinnah, founder of Pakistan.

Devon Avenue shows *pluralism*, the idea that many groups with different faiths and backgrounds can live side by side as equals. Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs, Jews and Christians shop on the same street. India and Pakistan have a long and tense history. Yet here, their emigrants run businesses next to each other and serve each other's families.

Ukrainian Village, west of downtown, grew in the early 1900s as Ukrainian immigrants arrived. The golden domes of St. Nicholas Ukrainian Catholic Cathedral rise over the neighborhood. The Ukrainian National Museum and churches keep traditions alive, such as pysanky, eggs decorated with wax and dye for Easter.

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the neighborhood has held rallies and collected aid. Longtime families have also welcomed new arrivals fleeing the war. The neighborhood has changed too, with many young residents of every background. Chicago's neighborhoods show that *identity* can be both deeply rooted and open to change.

words.d: the idea that many groups with different faiths and backgrounds can live together as equals
a person's sense of who they are, shaped by family, culture, faith, language and experience
Ukrainian Easter eggs decorated with wax and dye in detailed patterns

look.title: Mapping Your Identity
look.text: Mateo, from the chapter story, draws a map of his identity. At the center: Mexican American and Chicagoan. Around it: Spanish at home, English at school, Catholic, soccer fan, K-pop listener, grandson of a cook from Michoacán, friend of a classmate whose family runs a shop on Devon Avenue.
look.prompt: Which parts of Mateo's identity come from family, and which from the wider city? Sketch or list your own identity map.

check.q: What does pluralism mean?
choices: Many groups living together as equals
check.why: Pluralism is the idea that different faiths and backgrounds can live side by side as equals, as on Devon Avenue.

check.q: Which communities are described on Devon Avenue?
choices: South Asian businesses alongside a long-standing Jewish community
check.why: The reading says immigrants from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh share Devon Avenue with a Jewish community.

check.q: How has Ukrainian Village responded since 2022?
choices: It held rallies, collected aid and welcomed new arrivals
check.why: The reading says the neighborhood held rallies, collected aid and welcomed people fleeing the war.

review.q: Which is the best example of globalization of culture?
choices: A town that bans foreign films
Fans in Brazil singing BTS songs in Korean
review.why: Globalization is the spread of culture across borders, like Korean pop music reaching Brazil.

review.q: How are reggaeton and Bollywood alike?
choices: Both are sung only in English
Both grew from local roots into global styles by mixing traditions
review.why: Each is an example of cultural hybridity that grew from a local scene to a world audience.

review.q: A family leaves home because of war. The war is a:
review.why: Push factors drive people away, and war is a leading example.

review.q: Which policy asks newcomers to blend into one mainstream culture?
review.why: Assimilation, pictured as a melting pot, asks newcomers to adopt the main culture.

review.q: The kōhanga reo in New Zealand and Welsh in every school in Wales are both examples of:
review.why: Both are efforts to bring a fading language back into daily use.

review.q: Which is a right affirmed by the 2007 UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples?
choices: The right to leave any country
The right to a college degree
The right to be consulted on projects that affect their lands
review.why: The Declaration affirms rights to culture, language and land, and to be consulted on projects.

review.q: Which Chicago neighborhood was named after a city in Bohemia?
review.why: Czech immigrants named Pilsen after Plzeň, a city in Bohemia.

review.q: What question can help decide whether a use of culture is exchange or appropriation?
choices: Is the item sacred, and does the group get credit?
review.why: The reading suggests asking whether an item is sacred and whether its group gets credit or shares profit.
